events.label: Holmes and Watson sit by the fire in Baker Street lodgings
Holmes speaks about life being stranger than imagination

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: life is infinitely stranger than anything which the mind of man could invent; the things really commonplaces of existence are beyond conception; if people could hover over the city and peep in at what is going on, fiction would seem stale and unprofitable.

events.label: Watson says he is not convinced

communicates.speaker: narrator_doctor_watson
communicates.content: I am not convinced of it.

events.label: Watson describes cases in the papers and police reports as ordinary

communicates.speaker: narrator_doctor_watson
communicates.content: The cases which come to light in the papers are, as a rule, bald enough, and vulgar enough; police reports are realism pushed to its extreme limits and are neither fascinating nor artistic.

events.label: Holmes says selection and discretion are needed for realism

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: A certain selection and discretion must be used in producing a realistic effect; the police report lacks this and lays stress on platitudes rather than details.

events.label: Watson smiles and shakes his head
Watson says he understands Holmes's view

communicates.speaker: narrator_doctor_watson
communicates.content: I can quite understand your thinking so.

events.label: Watson mentions Holmes's role as adviser and helper

communicates.speaker: narrator_doctor_watson
communicates.content: In your position of unofficial adviser and helper to everybody who is absolutely puzzled, throughout three continents, you are brought in contact with all that is strange and bizarre.

events.label: Watson picks up the morning paper and proposes a practical test

communicates.speaker: narrator_doctor_watson
communicates.content: Let us put it to a practical test; here is the first heading upon which I come.

events.label: Watson cites a newspaper headline about a husband's cruelty to his wife

communicates.speaker: narrator_doctor_watson
communicates.content: A husband's cruelty to his wife; there is half a column of print and it is all perfectly familiar to me; there is, of course, the other woman, the drink, the push, the blow, the bruise, the sympathetic sister or landlady.

events.label: Holmes takes the paper and replies that the example is unfortunate

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: Indeed, your example is an unfortunate one for your argument.

events.label: Holmes identifies the Dundas separation case and describes its facts

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: This is the Dundas separation case; I was engaged in clearing up some small points in connection with it; the husband was a teetotaler, there was no other woman, and he had drifted into the habit of winding up every meal by taking out his false teeth and hurling them at his wife.

events.label: Holmes offers Watson snuff and claims to have scored over him

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: Take a pinch of snuff, Doctor, and acknowledge that I have scored over you in your example.

events.label: Holmes shows his snuffbox
Holmes explains the snuffbox is a souvenir from the King of Bohemia

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: I forgot that I had not seen you for some weeks; the snuffbox is a little souvenir from the King of Bohemia in return for my assistance in the case of the Irene Adler papers.

events.label: Watson asks about the ring

communicates.speaker: narrator_doctor_watson
communicates.content: And the ring?

events.label: Holmes explains the ring came from the reigning family of Holland

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: It was from the reigning family of Holland, though the matter in which I served them was of such delicacy that I cannot confide it even to you.

events.label: Watson asks whether Holmes has any case on hand just now

communicates.speaker: narrator_doctor_watson
communicates.content: Have you any on hand just now?

events.label: Sherlock Holmes observes a woman waiting outside the lodgings and she hurries across the road to ring the bell
Sherlock Holmes comments on the woman's symptoms and infers that she has a love matter

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: I have seen those symptoms before. Oscillation upon the pavement always means an affaire de coeur. She would like advice, but is not sure that the matter is not too delicate for communication. When a woman has been seriously wronged by a man she no longer oscillates, and the usual symptom is a broken bell wire. Here we may take it that there is a love matter, but that the maiden is not so much angry as perplexed, or grieved. But here she comes in person to resolve our doubts.

events.label: Mary Sutherland enters and Sherlock Holmes welcomes her into the room
Sherlock Holmes asks Mary Sutherland about her short sight and typewriting

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: Do you not find that with your short sight it is a little trying to do so much typewriting?

events.label: Mary Sutherland answers that she can now type without looking at the letters

communicates.speaker: miss_mary_sutherland
communicates.content: I did at first, but now I know where the letters are without looking.

events.label: Mary Sutherland reacts with fear and astonishment to Holmes's implication

communicates.speaker: miss_mary_sutherland
communicates.content: You’ve heard about me, Mr. Holmes, else how could you know all that?

events.label: Holmes replies that it is his business to know things and suggests the purpose of her visit

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: Never mind. It is my business to know things. Perhaps I have trained myself to see what others overlook. If not, why should you come to consult me?

events.label: Mary Sutherland says she came because of Mrs. Etherege and asks Holmes to help find Hosmer Angel

communicates.speaker: miss_mary_sutherland
communicates.content: I came to you, sir, because I heard of you from Mrs. Etherege, whose husband you found so easy when the police and everyone had given him up for dead. Oh, Mr. Holmes, I wish you would do as much for me. I’m not rich, but still I have a hundred a year in my own right, besides the little that I make by the machine, and I would give it all to know what has become of Mr. Hosmer Angel.

events.label: Holmes asks why Mary Sutherland came away to consult him in such a hurry

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: Why did you come away to consult me in such a hurry?

events.label: Mary Sutherland says she left the house in anger

communicates.speaker: miss_mary_sutherland
communicates.content: Yes, I did bang out of the house, for it made me angry to see the easy way in which Mr. Windibank—that is, my father—took it all. He would not go to the police, and he would not go to you, and so at last, as he would do nothing and kept on saying that there was no harm done, it made me mad, and I just on with my things and came right away to you.

events.label: Holmes clarifies that Mr. Windibank is her stepfather

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: Your father, your stepfather, surely, since the name is different.

events.label: Mary Sutherland states that her mother is alive and well

communicates.speaker: miss_mary_sutherland
communicates.content: Oh, yes, mother is alive and well.

events.label: Mary Sutherland describes her father's death, her mother's remarriage, and the sale of the business

communicates.speaker: miss_mary_sutherland
communicates.content: I wasn’t best pleased, Mr. Holmes, when she married again so soon after father’s death, and a man who was nearly fifteen years younger than herself. Father was a plumber in the Tottenham Court Road, and he left a tidy business behind him, which mother carried on with Mr. Hardy, the foreman; but when Mr. Windibank came he made her sell the business, for he was very superior, being a traveller in wines. They got £4700 for the goodwill and interest, which wasn’t near as much as father could have got if he had been alive.

events.label: Holmes asks about Mary Sutherland's income

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: Your own little income, does it come out of the business?

events.label: Mary Sutherland explains that her income is separate and came from her uncle

communicates.speaker: miss_mary_sutherland
communicates.content: Oh, no, sir. It is quite separate and was left me by my uncle Ned in Auckland. It is in New Zealand stock, paying 41/2 per cent. Two thousand five hundred pounds was the amount, but I can only touch the interest.

events.label: Holmes comments on Mary Sutherland's income and spending

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: You interest me extremely. And since you draw so large a sum as a hundred a year, with what you earn into the bargain, you no doubt travel a little and indulge yourself in every way. I believe that a single lady can get on very nicely upon an income of about £60.

events.label: Mary Sutherland explains that her family uses her money while she lives at home and that Windibank pays her interest to her mother

communicates.speaker: miss_mary_sutherland
communicates.content: I could do with much less than that, Mr. Holmes, but you understand that as long as I live at home I don’t wish to be a burden to them, and so they have the use of the money just while I am staying with them. Of course, that is only just for the time. Mr. Windibank draws my interest every quarter and pays it over to mother, and I find that I can do pretty well with what I earn at typewriting. It brings me twopence a sheet, and I can often do from fifteen to twenty sheets in a day.

events.label: Holmes asks Mary Sutherland to explain her connection with Hosmer Angel

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: This is my friend, Dr. Watson, before whom you can speak as freely as before myself. Kindly tell us now all about your connection with Mr. Hosmer Angel.

events.label: Mary Sutherland states that she met Hosmer Angel at the gasfitters' ball

communicates.speaker: miss_mary_sutherland
communicates.content: I met him first at the gasfitters’ ball.

events.label: Mary Sutherland says the gasfitters sent tickets to her family and that Windibank objected to their going

communicates.speaker: miss_mary_sutherland
communicates.content: They used to send father tickets when he was alive, and then afterwards they remembered us, and sent them to mother. Mr. Windibank did not wish us to go. He never did wish us to go anywhere. He would get quite mad if I wanted so much as to join a Sunday-school treat. But this time I was set on going, and I would go; for what right had he to prevent? He said the folk were not fit for us to know, when all father’s friends were to be there. And he said that I had nothing fit to wear, when I had my purple plush that I had never so much as taken out of the drawer.

events.label: Mr. Windibank returns from France and reacts to Mary Sutherland having gone to the ball

communicates.speaker: mr_windibank
communicates.content: There is no use denying anything to a woman, for she will have her way.

events.label: Mary Sutherland meets Hosmer Angel at the gasfitters' ball
Hosmer Angel calls next day to ask whether Mary Sutherland and her mother got home safely

communicates.speaker: hosmer_angel
communicates.content: to ask if we had got home all safe

events.label: Mary Sutherland and Hosmer Angel meet twice for walks
Father returns and Hosmer Angel can no longer come to the house
Hosmer Angel writes to say not to see each other until father has gone

communicates.speaker: hosmer_angel
communicates.content: it would be safer and better not to see each other until he had gone; we can write in the meantime

events.label: Hosmer Angel writes daily letters to Mary Sutherland

communicates.speaker: hosmer_angel
communicates.content: we could write in the meantime

events.label: Mary Sutherland and Hosmer Angel become engaged after their first walk
Hosmer Angel is described as a cashier in an office on Leadenhall Street
Mary Sutherland addresses letters to the Leadenhall Street Post Office
Hosmer Angel refuses typed letters and says they would feel impersonal

communicates.speaker: hosmer_angel
communicates.content: if they were sent to the office he would be chaffed by all the other clerks about having letters from a lady; when I wrote them they seemed to come from me, but when they were typewritten the machine had come between us

events.label: Holmes comments that the little things are most important

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: It has long been an axiom of mine that the little things are infinitely the most important.

events.label: Mary Sutherland describes Hosmer Angel as shy, retiring, and weak-throated

communicates.speaker: miss_mary_sutherland
communicates.content: He was a very shy man; he preferred evening walks, hated to be conspicuous, had a weak throat and a hesitating, whispering speech, and wore tinted glasses.

events.label: Hosmer Angel returns to the house and proposes marriage before father comes back

communicates.speaker: hosmer_angel
communicates.content: we should marry before father came back; whatever happened you would always be true to me

events.label: Mary asks about her father before the planned wedding

communicates.speaker: miss_mary_sutherland
communicates.content: Then, when they talked of marrying within the week, I began to ask about father; but they both said never to mind about father, but just to tell him afterwards, and mother said she would make it all right with him.

events.label: Mary writes to her father at Bordeaux

communicates.speaker: miss_mary_sutherland
communicates.content: I wrote to father at Bordeaux, where the company has its French offices.

events.label: Father starts to England before the letter arrives
Mary and Hosmer's wedding is arranged for Friday
Mary and Hosmer arrive at St. Saviour's by cab
Hosmer disappears before stepping out of the four-wheeler
Holmes says Mary has been shamefully treated

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: It seems to me that you have been very shamefully treated.

events.label: Hosmer speaks to Mary on the wedding morning about remaining true and being pledged

communicates.speaker: hosmer_angel
communicates.content: whatever happened, I was to be true; and that even if something quite unforeseen occurred to separate us, I was always to remember that I was pledged to him, and that he would claim his pledge sooner or later.

events.label: Holmes asks whether an unforeseen catastrophe occurred

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: Your own opinion is, then, that some unforeseen catastrophe has occurred to him?

events.label: Mary says she has no notion what happened to Hosmer

communicates.speaker: miss_mary_sutherland
communicates.content: Yes, sir. I believe that he foresaw some danger, or else he would not have talked so. And then I think that what he foresaw happened. None.

events.label: Holmes asks how Mary's mother took the matter

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: One more question. How did your mother take the matter?

events.label: Mary says her mother was angry and forbade further mention

communicates.speaker: miss_mary_sutherland
communicates.content: She was angry, and said that I was never to speak of the matter again.

events.label: Holmes asks whether Mary told her father

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: And your father? Did you tell him?

events.label: Mary says her father expected to hear of Hosmer again

communicates.speaker: miss_mary_sutherland
communicates.content: Yes; and he seemed to think, with me, that something had happened, and that I should hear of Hosmer again. As he said, what interest could anyone have in bringing me to the doors of the church, and then leaving me? Now, if he had borrowed my money, or if he had married me and got my money settled on him, there might be some reason, but Hosmer was very independent about money and never would look at a shilling of mine. And yet, what could have happened? And why could he not write? Oh, it drives me half-mad to think of it, and I can’t sleep a wink at night.

events.label: Mary sobs into her handkerchief
Holmes says he will examine the case and asks for time to work

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: I shall glance into the case for you, and we shall reach some definite result. Let the weight of the matter rest upon me now. Let Mr. Hosmer Angel vanish from your memory. Leave that question in my hands. I should like an accurate description of him and any letters of his which you can spare. You will leave the papers here, and remember the advice which I have given you. Let the whole incident be a sealed book, and do not allow it to affect your life.

events.label: Mary Sutherland asks whether she will see Hosmer Angel again and what happened to him

communicates.speaker: miss_mary_sutherland
communicates.content: Then you don’t think I’ll see him again? Then what has happened to him?

events.label: Holmes says he fears Mary Sutherland will not see Hosmer Angel again

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: I fear not.

events.label: Mary Sutherland provides a newspaper slip and four letters from Hosmer Angel

communicates.speaker: miss_mary_sutherland
communicates.content: I advertised for him in last Saturday’s Chronicle. Here is the slip and here are four letters from him.

events.label: Holmes asks for Mary Sutherland’s address and her father’s place of business

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: And your address? Mr. Angel’s address you never had, I understand. Where is your father’s place of business?

events.label: Mary Sutherland gives her address and identifies her father’s employer

communicates.speaker: miss_mary_sutherland
communicates.content: 31 Lyon Place, Camberwell. He travels for Westhouse & Marbank, the great claret importers of Fenchurch Street.

events.label: Mary Sutherland refuses Holmes’s advice and pledges loyalty to Hosmer Angel

communicates.speaker: miss_mary_sutherland
communicates.content: You are very kind, Mr. Holmes, but I cannot do that. I shall be true to Hosmer. He shall find me ready when he comes back.

events.label: Mary Sutherland leaves her papers and departs, promising to return if summoned
Holmes sits silent, smokes his pipe, and contemplates the woman
Holmes comments that the maiden is an interesting study

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: Quite an interesting study, that maiden. I found her more interesting than her little problem, which is rather a trite one. You will find parallel cases, if you consult my index, in Andover in ’77, and there was something of the sort at The Hague last year. Old as is the idea, however, there were one or two details which were new to me. But the maiden herself was most instructive.

events.label: Watson says Holmes read details on the woman that were invisible to him

communicates.speaker: narrator_doctor_watson
communicates.content: You appeared to read a good deal upon her which was quite invisible to me.

events.label: Holmes explains Watson missed important signs and asks him to describe the woman’s appearance

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: Not invisible but unnoticed, Watson. You did not know where to look, and so you missed all that was important. I can never bring you to realise the importance of sleeves, the suggestiveness of thumb-nails, or the great issues that may hang from a boot-lace. Now, what did you gather from that woman’s appearance? Describe it.

events.label: Watson describes the woman’s appearance

communicates.speaker: narrator_doctor_watson
communicates.content: She had a slate-coloured, broad-brimmed straw hat, with a feather of a brickish red. Her jacket was black, with black beads sewn upon it, and a fringe of little black jet ornaments. Her dress was brown, rather darker than coffee colour, with a little purple plush at the neck and sleeves. Her gloves were greyish and were worn through at the right forefinger. She had small round, hanging gold earrings, and a general air of being fairly well-to-do in a vulgar, comfortable, easy-going way.

events.label: Holmes reacts with soft applause and laughter
Holmes praises Watson for his method and attention to detail

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: You are coming along wonderfully. You have really done very well indeed. It is true that you have missed everything of importance, but you have hit upon the method, and you have a quick eye for colour. Never trust to general impressions, my boy, but concentrate yourself upon details.

events.label: Holmes explains his observational method for women and men

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: My first glance is always at a woman’s sleeve. In a man it is perhaps better first to take the knee of the trouser.

events.label: Holmes describes the woman's sleeve marks and typewriting traces

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: This woman had plush upon her sleeves. The double line above the wrist was beautifully defined. The sewing-machine leaves a similar mark, but only on the left arm. I glanced at her face, saw the dint of a pince-nez, and ventured a remark upon short sight and typewriting.

events.label: Watson says the observation surprised him

communicates.speaker: narrator_doctor_watson
communicates.content: It surprised me.

events.label: Holmes explains the odd boots and hurried departure

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: It was obvious. The boots were odd ones and half-buttoned. When a young lady otherwise neatly dressed has come away from home with odd boots, half-buttoned, she came away in a hurry.

events.label: Watson asks what else Holmes observed

communicates.speaker: narrator_doctor_watson
communicates.content: And what else?

events.label: Holmes describes the note and violet-ink stain on the glove and finger

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: She had written a note before leaving home but after being fully dressed. Her right glove was torn at the forefinger, and both glove and finger were stained with violet ink. She had written in a hurry and dipped her pen too deep. It must have been this morning, or the mark would not remain clear upon the finger.

events.label: Holmes asks Watson to read the advertised description of Hosmer Angel

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: I must go back to business, Watson. Would you mind reading me the advertised description of Mr. Hosmer Angel?

events.label: Watson reads the advertisement describing Hosmer Angel

communicates.speaker: narrator_doctor_watson
communicates.content: Missing, on the morning of the fourteenth, a gentleman named Hosmer Angel. About five ft. seven in. in height; strongly built, sallow complexion, black hair, a little bald in the centre, bushy, black side-whiskers and moustache; tinted glasses, slight infirmity of speech. Was dressed, when last seen, in black frock-coat faced with silk, black waistcoat, gold Albert chain, and grey Harris tweed trousers, with brown gaiters over elastic-sided boots. Known to have been employed in an office in Leadenhall Street. Anybody bringing—

events.label: Holmes examines the letters and comments on their typewritten signature

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: The letters are very commonplace. There is absolutely no clue in them to Mr. Angel, save that he quotes Balzac once. The point about the signature is very suggestive and may be called conclusive. I shall write two letters, one to a firm in the City and the other to the young lady’s stepfather, Mr. Windibank, asking him whether he could meet us here at six o’clock tomorrow evening.

events.label: Holmes and Watson put the little problem aside until the answers arrive
Watson leaves Holmes and later returns to Baker Street
Holmes spends the day working with chemicals
Watson asks Holmes whether he has solved the mystery

communicates.speaker: narrator_doctor_watson
communicates.content: Well, have you solved it?

events.label: Holmes answers that the substance was bisulphate of baryta

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: It was the bisulphate of baryta.

events.label: Watson asks who the man was and what his object was in deserting Miss Sutherland

communicates.speaker: narrator_doctor_watson
communicates.content: Who was he, then, and what was his object in deserting Miss Sutherland?

events.label: Holmes announces that Windibank is the girl's stepfather and has written to arrive at six

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: This is the girl’s stepfather, Mr. James Windibank. He has written to me to say that he would be here at six. Come in!

events.label: Mr. James Windibank enters the room and sits down
Holmes greets Windibank and identifies the typewritten letter as his

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: Good-evening, Mr. James Windibank. I think that this typewritten letter is from you, in which you made an appointment with me for six o’clock?

events.label: Windibank apologizes for being late and remarks on Miss Sutherland's trouble

communicates.speaker: mr_james_windibank
communicates.content: Yes, sir. I am afraid that I am a little late, but I am not quite my own master, you know. I am sorry that Miss Sutherland has troubled you about this little matter, for I think it is far better not to wash linen of the sort in public. It was quite against my wishes that she came, but she is a very excitable, impulsive girl, as you may have noticed, and she is not easily controlled when she has made up her mind on a point.

events.label: Holmes states that he will succeed in discovering Hosmer Angel

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: I have every reason to believe that I will succeed in discovering Mr. Hosmer Angel.

events.label: Mr. Windibank gives a violent start and drops his gloves
Holmes remarks on the individuality of typewriters and describes worn letters

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: It is a curious thing that a typewriter has really quite as much individuality as a man’s handwriting. Unless they are quite new, no two of them write exactly alike. Some letters get more worn than others, and some wear only on one side. Now, you remark in this note of yours, Mr. Windibank, that in every case there is some little slurring over of the ‘e,’ and a slight defect in the tail of the ‘r.’ There are fourteen other characteristics, but those are the more obvious.

events.label: Mr. Windibank says his office uses the machine for all correspondence

communicates.speaker: mr_windibank
communicates.content: We do all our correspondence with this machine at the office, and no doubt it is a little worn.

events.label: Holmes says he will show Windibank an interesting study and mentions a monograph on typewriters and crime

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: And now I will show you what is really a very interesting study, Mr. Windibank. I think of writing another little monograph some of these days on the typewriter and its relation to crime. It is a subject to which I have devoted some little attention.

events.label: Holmes produces four letters that purport to come from the missing man and says they are type-written

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: I have here four letters which purport to come from the missing man. They are all type-written. In each case, not only are the ‘e’s’ slurred and the ‘r’s’ tailless, but the fourteen other characteristics to which I have alluded are there as well.

events.label: Mr. Windibank stands up, picks up his hat, and refuses to stay for the discussion

communicates.speaker: mr_windibank
communicates.content: I cannot waste time over this sort of fantastic talk, Mr. Holmes. If you can catch the man, catch him, and let me know when you have done it.

events.label: Holmes turns the key in the door and says he has caught the man

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: Certainly. I let you know, then, that I have caught him!

events.label: Mr. Windibank asks where the man is

communicates.speaker: mr_windibank
communicates.content: What! where?

events.label: Holmes tells Windibank that escape is impossible and orders him to sit down

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: Oh, it won’t do—really it won’t. There is no possible getting out of it, Mr. Windibank. It is quite too transparent, and it was a very bad compliment when you said that it was impossible for me to solve so simple a question. That’s right! Sit down and let us talk it over.

events.label: Windibank collapses into a chair
Windibank says the matter is not actionable

communicates.speaker: mr_windibank
communicates.content: It’s not actionable.

events.label: Holmes says the matter is not actionable and condemns the trick

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: I am very much afraid that it is not. But between ourselves, Windibank, it was as cruel and selfish and heartless a trick in a petty way as ever came before me.

events.label: Holmes begins to run over the course of events
Holmes states that the man married for money and used the daughter's money while she lived with them

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: The man married a woman very much older than himself for her money, and he enjoyed the use of the money of the daughter as long as she lived with them. It was a considerable sum, for people in their position, and the loss of it would have made a serious difference. It was worth an effort to preserve it.

events.label: The stepfather keeps the girl at home and forbids her to seek company of people her own age
The girl becomes restive and announces her intention to go to a ball
Mr. Windibank disguises himself as Hosmer Angel with his wife's help
Hosmer Angel begins calling on the girl
The girl and Hosmer Angel meet and become engaged
Mr. Windibank brings the girl as far as the church door and then vanishes by stepping through the four-wheeler
Mr. Windibank denies wrongdoing and accuses Holmes of unlawful restraint

communicates.speaker: mr_windibank_stepfather
communicates.content: It may be so, or it may not, Mr. Holmes, but if you are so very sharp you ought to be sharp enough to know that it is you who are breaking the law now, and not me. I have done nothing actionable from the first, but as long as you keep that door locked you lay yourself open to an action for assault and illegal constraint.

events.label: Holmes unlocks the door and opens it
Holmes condemns Mr. Windibank and threatens him with a hunting crop

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: The law cannot, as you say, touch you, yet there never was a man who deserved punishment more. If the young lady has a brother or a friend, he ought to lay a whip across your shoulders. By Jove! it is not part of my duties to my client, but here’s a hunting crop handy, and I think I shall just treat myself to—

events.label: Holmes laughs and describes the man as a cold-blooded scoundrel

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: There’s a cold-blooded scoundrel! That fellow will rise from crime to crime until he does something very bad, and ends on a gallows. The case has, in some respects, been not entirely devoid of interest.

events.label: Watson says he cannot fully see Holmes's reasoning

communicates.speaker: narrator_doctor_watson
communicates.content: I cannot now entirely see all the steps of your reasoning.

events.label: Holmes explains how he inferred the stepfather and the disguise

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: It was obvious from the first that this Mr. Hosmer Angel must have some strong object for his curious conduct, and it was equally clear that the only man who really profited by the incident, as far as we could see, was the stepfather. Then the fact that the two men were never together, but that the one always appeared when the other was away, was suggestive. So were the tinted spectacles and the curious voice, which both hinted at a disguise, as did the bushy whiskers. My suspicions were all confirmed by his peculiar action in typewriting his signature, which inferred that his handwriting was so familiar to her that she would recognise even the smallest sample of it. You see all these isolated facts, together with many minor ones, all pointed in the same direction.

events.label: Watson asks how Holmes verified the facts

communicates.speaker: narrator_doctor_watson
communicates.content: And how did you verify them?

events.label: Holmes explains how he sent the description and wrote to the man

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: Having once spotted my man, it was easy to get corroboration. I knew the firm for which this man worked. Having taken the printed description, I eliminated everything from it which could be the result of a disguise—the whiskers, the glasses, the voice, and I sent it to the firm, with a request that they would inform me whether it answered to the description of any of their travellers. I had already noticed the peculiarities of the typewriter, and I wrote to the man himself at his business address asking him if he would come here. As I expected, his reply was typewritten and revealed the same trivial but characteristic defects. The same post brought me a letter from Westhouse & Marbank, of Fenchurch Street, to say that the description tallied in every respect with that of their employee, James Windibank. Voil `a tout!

events.label: Watson asks about Miss Sutherland

communicates.speaker: narrator_doctor_watson
communicates.content: And Miss Sutherland?

events.label: Holmes says Miss Sutherland will not believe him and quotes a Persian saying

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: If I tell her she will not believe me. You may remember the old Persian saying, ‘There is danger for him who taketh the tiger cub, and danger also for whoso snatches a delusion from a woman.’ There is as much sense in Hafiz as in Horace, and as much knowledge of the world.

clues.significance: Mary's letter to her father arrived back on the morning of the wedding because father had already started to England.
Holmes inferred that the signature was not handwritten because it was typewritten, and treated that as conclusive for the case.
Holmes inferred that Mary Sutherland had written in a hurry and dipped her pen too deep because her glove and finger were stained with violet ink.
Holmes identified the chemical he had been working upon as bisulphate of baryta.
Holmes inferred that the letters were linked by the same worn typewriter because the slurred 'e's', tailless 'r's', and fourteen other matching characteristics appeared in each one.
Holmes inferred that Mr. Windibank had been impersonating Hosmer Angel from the disguise and the staged appearances.
Holmes inferred that the handwriting was familiar to Miss Sutherland from the man's peculiar typewriting of his signature.
